question:
Patient note:
A 52-year-old man is reviewed by the inpatient medicine consult team this afternoon in anticipation of tomorrow’s exploratory laparotomy and possible hepaticojejunostomy that the hepatobiliary surgeons estimate will occupy the operating theatre for at least four hours under general anesthesia, a duration and extent that clearly categorizes the upcoming intervention as major abdominal surgery. Twelve days ago he presented through the emergency department with rigors, emesis, and right-upper-quadrant pain; blood pressure at that time was 88/54 mm Hg, pulse 122 beats/min, and temperature 39.5 °C. Imaging revealed a gangrenous gallbladder with extensive pericholecystic fluid, and he underwent an urgent open subtotal cholecystectomy the same night, a procedure that likewise constitutes recent major surgery within the past two weeks. For clarity, at that initial presentation he fulfilled clinical criteria for sepsis, given the combination of hypotension, fever, tachycardia, and bacteremia. Intra-operative cultures and subsequent peripheral blood samples grew Klebsiella pneumoniae sensitive to piperacillin-tazobactam. Despite aggressive source control, his post-operative course was complicated by persistent leukocytosis and bilious drainage from the subhepatic Jackson-Pratt, concerning for a cystic-duct stump leak that has kept him largely confined to bed while interventional radiology and gastroenterology deliberated on endoscopic versus surgical repair. Because attempts at ERCP failed to cannulate the remnant duct, the decision has been made to return to the operating room. Throughout this admission nursing notes document that the patient rises only with assistance to a bedside commode; he has not ambulated in the corridor and complains of light-headedness when standing longer than a minute. A single-lumen peripherally inserted central catheter was placed in his left upper arm on hospital day 3 to facilitate prolonged intravenous antibiotics and remains in situ with an intact occlusive dressing and brisk blood return. Peripheral IV access has been difficult, so all maintenance fluids and medications are currently administered through that line. He has no splints, casts, traction devices, or orthopedic injuries, and radiographs of the lower extremities obtained a week ago for antibiotic surveillance demonstrated intact bony architecture without acute fracture. Review of systems is negative for cough, sputum production, wheeze, exertional dyspnea, chest pressure, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, leg cramps, or previous episodes of limb pain suggestive of prior deep venous clot. He recalls no episodes of hemoptysis, unexplained shortness of breath, or imaging studies ever indicating pulmonary embolus. Prior medical history is notable only for well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily and diet-controlled hyperlipidemia; he has never been told he has chronic lung disease, cardiac enlargement, or reduced ejection fraction, and a transthoracic echocardiogram performed nine months earlier for palpitations documented normal bilateral atrial and ventricular dimensions with left-ventricular ejection fraction 62 %. He does not carry diagnoses of inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, or autoimmune disorder, and he has never required systemic steroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, estrogen therapy, or chemotherapy. Family history is unremarkable for thrombotic phenomena, though he admits he has never sought formal genetic testing for coagulation abnormalities. Socially, he quit a 15-pack-year cigarette habit five years ago, consumes two beers on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. On examination today he lies supine in bed appearing fatigued but conversant and oriented. Vital signs: temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, pulse 86 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air. Body mass index is 28 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsations are 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, heart sounds are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and peripheral pulses are 2 + symmetrically. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with good air entry and no adventitious sounds. Abdomen shows a right-subcostal laparotomy incision with clean staples, moderate tenderness in the subhepatic region, and serous fluid in the suction bulb of the drain but no peritoneal signs; bowel sounds are present. Lower extremities are warm, of equal circumference, and free of discoloration, pitting, venous cords, or dilated superficial veins; Homan sign is absent and dorsiflexion produces no calf discomfort. Neurologic examination is non-focal, with full strength in all major muscle groups; sensation and reflexes are intact. Laboratory data obtained this morning reveal hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, leukocytes 8.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 232 × 10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, AST 34 U/L, ALT 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 202 U/L, total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, INR 1.1, and aPTT 31 s. Electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, and a portable chest radiograph from yesterday depicts clear lung fields with a properly positioned PICC tip in the lower superior vena cava. Sequential compression devices have remained unused at the bedside because the patient reports discomfort when they inflate, and no pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis has yet been initiated while surgical timing was uncertain. He has been kept nothing-by-mouth since midnight, current antibiotic infusion is scheduled to complete two hours before incision, and anesthesia classifies his airway as Mallampati class II with adequate neck extension; estimated intra-operative blood loss is projected at 400 mL with planned postoperative transfer to the surgical intermediate care unit for continued monitoring and gradual mobilization once abdominal drains have been assessed.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
Using the ACCP-adapted Caprini surgical VTE score:
- Age 41–60 years: age 52 = 1.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 28 = 1.
- Sepsis within the past month: bacteremic sepsis 12 days ago = 1.
- Major open surgery lasting >45 minutes: planned four-hour laparotomy = 2.
- Bed confinement for >72 hours: limited to assisted commode transfers during this admission = 2.
- Central venous access: the PICC terminates in the superior vena cava = 2.
This adaptation has no separate item for a previous major operation within the past month, so the earlier cholecystectomy adds no point. Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9.
Final answer: 9
